CVE-2025-24337.title: WriteFreely through 0.15.1, when MySQL is used, allows local user ...
CVE-2025-24337.description: WriteFreely through 0.15.1, when MySQL is used, allows local users to discover credentials by reading config.ini.

GHSA-22qx-x758-m72p.title: IPv6 transition address bypass of SSRF guards around ActivityPub federation
GHSA-22qx-x758-m72p.description: ## Summary When federation is enabled on an instance, certain safeguards to prevent the server from making requests to internal or private network addresses weren't hardened against certain IPv6 formats that could be used to bypass these safeguards. This is a follow-up fix to GHSA-wvrr-gx9p-xvxm and GHSA-7635-vx4w-qww7. ## Credit Reported by tonghuaroot (tonghuaroot@gmail.com).

GHSA-7635-vx4w-qww7.title: Unauthenticated SSRF via ActivityPub inbox actor/object IRI resolution
GHSA-7635-vx4w-qww7.description: ### Summary WriteFreely's federation feature could've been tricked into sending network requests to internal systems that should be off-limits from the outside. By crafting a malicious identifier, an attacker could've redirected the server's own outbound requests toward private infrastructure instead of the intended remote server.

GHSA-7jv7-gf23-wcqq.title: Unauthenticated auth bypass via API access tokens
GHSA-7jv7-gf23-wcqq.description: ### Summary A flaw in how WriteFreely checked API access tokens could've let an unauthenticated attacker use the API as another user, without that user's password or access token. Any account with an active API access token could be impersonated. That includes tokens created by logging in through a desktop or mobile app, a command-line client, or another API integration, and it could include the instance administrator's account. ### Impact **This is a critical issue.** It could be exploited remotely by anyone, with no account on the instance, no action from the victim, and very little effort. An attacker who took over an account this way could read everything the account owner can read, including drafts, private posts, and posts in private or password-protected blogs. They could also create, edit, or delete posts and blogs as that user. All WriteFreely instances running 0.17.2 or earlier are affected, on both MySQL / MariaDB and SQLite deployments, as long as at least one user has an active API access token. ### After upgrading Upgrading prevents the bypass, but it doesn't revoke any access an attacker may have gained before you upgraded. We recommend that admins: - Revoke all existing API access tokens. This signs people out of apps and API clients, but not the web. - Optionally, regenerate your session keys to sign everyone out on the web as well. - Check that the email addresses on admin accounts are correct. The [v0.17.3 release notes](https://github.com/writefreely/writefreely/releases/tag/v0.17.3) include instructions for each step. ### Credit Reported by diaoqi129.

GHSA-cwxm-8ch5-j2vh.title: Stored XSS via Unsanitized Post Slug in RSS / Email / ActivityPub Output
GHSA-cwxm-8ch5-j2vh.description: ## Summary The post creation API stores a user-supplied `slug` field verbatim without sanitization. When a post is in a Web-Monetized collection and contains the `<!--paid-->` shortcode, `augmentReadingDestination()` concatenates the raw slug into an HTML anchor tag wrapped in `template.HTML()`, bypassing Go's contextual auto-escaping.

GHSA-hwfg-mg9c-cvgf.title: WriteFreely: cross-user post pin/unpin IDOR lets any user rewrite another user's blog navigation
GHSA-hwfg-mg9c-cvgf.description: ### Summary On multi-user instances, any logged-in user could've pinned or unpinned another user's published posts. Pinned posts appear as links in a blog's navigation menu and don't appear in its main post list or feeds. An attacker could add links to another user's navigation menu, remove the pages the owner had pinned there, or hide individual posts from the blog's main page and feeds. The attacker couldn't read, edit, or delete another user's posts, or change any other blog settings. ### Impact This is a moderate-severity issue. It required an ordinary account on the instance, but nothing from the blog's owner, and it only affected how a blog's existing posts were displayed. Single-user instances without any other users aren't affected. ### Credit Reported by 5ud0 (Tarmo Technologies).
